assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms) opened a route to fractional frequency uncertainties near 1e-18, a genuine step in precision that rests on quantum-mechanical insight. They are now used for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic redshift over millimetre scales and prospects for redefining the second. This is atomic physics where theory and experiment agree quantitatively, which I value highly.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength idea and demonstrated the first lattice clock; Ye's group brought strontium lattice clocks to the highest accuracy and coherence. Both are clear, decisive contributors and a two-person prize is natural. The list gives no third name, and the ion-clock and comb communities (already recognised in 2005) are separate; I would regard the exact split of credit relative to Hall and Hansch work and ion clocks as settled enough.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) reproduce and improve the results, and clock comparisons are stable and cross-checked. Recognition is timely, with the redefinition of the second still pending.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to separate lattice clocks from earlier recognised comb and single-ion clock work.
I have not independently verified the latest published uncertainty figures.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling and controlling the motion of macroscopic mechanical oscillators into the quantum regime (ground state, squeezing, entanglement, quantum-limited readout) speaks directly to where the boundary between the quantum and classical worlds lies. This is a fundamental question rather than a technological one, and the work is conceptually clear and original. It follows naturally from recent recognition of macroscopic quantum phenomena.
assessment.attribution: Five credited names, which must be cut to at most three. Cleland (first mechanical quantum ground state, 2010) and Teufel (sideband cooling in circuit electromechanics, 2011) are decisive, as are Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg for cavity optomechanics, and Painter for nanobeam crystals. Any three leaves out someone with a strong claim; this is the main difficulty, and I would revisit the choice in discussion.
assessment.maturity: Results have been reproduced across superconducting, optical and phononic-crystal platforms with consistent interpretation. Applications to sensing are emerging, but the fundamental result is solid and the timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Unresolved allocation among five strong contributors across microwave and optical platforms.
Overlap with the 2025 prize theme may weigh for or against a near-term award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with cold atoms in optical lattices, including the observation of the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later single-site imaging, gives a controllable, clean realisation of many-body Hamiltonians. It lets us study strongly correlated quantum matter in ways that no solid-state system allows. The ideas are original and the impact on many-body physics is broad.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and collaborators) provided the theoretical proposals; Bloch and Greiner carried out landmark experiments (Mott transition, quantum gas microscopy). Cirac is also a major theoretical contributor to quantum simulation, and Hänsch-Greiner-Bloch lineage and Jaksch are not on the list, so credit is not wholly captured. The three names chosen form a sensible theory-plus-experiment configuration, but the credited set overlaps with other entries (B019, B031, B036) and credit for Zoller and Cirac would need coordinated handling.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced in many laboratories, with a mature field, though the most impressive applications to open physics questions are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap in laureate sets with trapped-ion and Rydberg entries could force a combined or exclusive decision.
Whether the discovery is best framed as a single advance or a broad programme.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought cavity-QED physics, which I know well from atoms, onto a chip with strong coupling of an artificial atom to a single microwave photon. It is both a clean platform for studying light-matter interaction and the basis of superconducting quantum processors. The idea is original and its influence is large.
assessment.attribution: Blais proposed the architecture with Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf; Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in 2004. Girvin and Huang are not on the list, so the credit is incomplete. Superconducting qubit foundations (Nakamura, Devoret, Martinis) already received recognition in 2025, which shapes how the distinct contribution is judged.
assessment.maturity: Highly reproduced and developing rapidly. Recognition is arguably timely, but the question of how far it is distinct from the 2025 award needs care.
uncertainties: Missing credited names (e.g. Girvin) in the supplied set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos by IceCube opened a new window on the universe, with the diffuse flux and later source associations (blazar TXS 0506+056, Galactic plane). It is a genuinely new observation about nature, not technologically motivated. I defer to colleagues on astroparticle physics for a finer judgement.
assessment.attribution: IceCube was a very large collaboration; Halzen is the scientific leader and driving visionary, and Karle a key figure in the detector design and operation. The supplied credit has only these two names, and other leaders (e.g. the spokespersons and the AMANDA pioneers) are not available, so the configuration is fair only if the committee accepts the leadership-based attribution.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is well established; source identification is still limited to a few cases, and KM3NeT results are still emerging. Recognition is reasonable but may be a little early for the source-astronomy part.
uncertainties: Collaboration-scale credit and the limited number of named laureates.
Strength of independent confirmation of individual source associations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Controlled strongly interacting Fermi gases (Feshbach-resonance tuning, the BEC-BCS crossover, observation of vortices and superfluidity) provide a universal quantum many-body system. They connect atomic physics to superconductivity and neutron-star matter in a clear way. The physics is fundamental and elegant.
assessment.attribution: Grimm, Salomon, Ketterle, Jin (deceased) and Thomas, among others, made the key experiments; the supplied set omits Deborah Jin, who would have been central, and so the fairness of the allocation is compromised. Ketterle is already a laureate (2001), which could reduce the case for including him.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally reproduced by many groups, with quantitative agreement with many-body theory. The field is mature and the recognition is, if anything, late.
uncertainties: Absence of Deborah Jin from the credited names and her death make the allocation difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators (the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells and three-dimensional topological insulators) added a new class of electronic states of matter, with robust edge or surface transport protected by symmetry. The theoretical prediction followed by decisive experiment is a model of fundamental discovery. It is outside my main field, so I weigh colleagues' views heavily.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical proposal, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang predicted HgTe, and Molenkamp's group observed the effect; Hasan and Moore, Balents, Fu also contributed to the three-dimensional case. The credited list has four names and misses Zhang, so allocation of credit is contested.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by numerous independent experiments and now a mature field, with the interpretation stable.
uncertainties: Contested allocation among theory proposals, the HgTe experiment and the three-dimensional materials.
Overlap with entry B039 on the same discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: X-ray free-electron lasers (SASE concept and the LCLS and FLASH/European XFEL realisations) provide femtosecond, intense, coherent X-ray pulses and have opened time-resolved structural and electronic dynamics on atomic scales. This relates closely to the ultrafast and attosecond science I work with. It is more an invention and a facility than a single discovery, which weighs against it somewhat.
assessment.attribution: The SASE concept is associated with Kondratenko-Saldin, Bonifacio-Pellegrini-Narducci and Kim, while the realisation of lasing involved large teams at DESY and SLAC. The supplied credited names may not cover all decisive contributors, and the allocation between concept and implementation is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Facilities operate worldwide, with broad scientific use, so confirmation is strong and recognition is timely, although the dominant impact is in other sciences.
uncertainties: Missing early theorists in the supplied credit set.
Whether the prize is for an instrument or a physics discovery.
